The reviewers all appreciated the fact that the novel LocoMouse tool permits automated analysis with high resolution of locomotion of freely walking mice, and they judged that this method has the potential to be of value to the field. They provide a number of comments for strengthening the manuscript, which are included below. These comments center on the being more explicit about the limits of the work, its interpretation (especially regarding the mutants), and comparison to other studies, providing more information about certain analyses, and addressing some points for clarity of presentation and communication. Specifically:

1) Toning down the claims about the superiority and power of the new method, perhaps providing a more explicit comparison to commercial packages.

2) Toning down the claims about providing direct evidence for forward models, perhaps simply by shifting these ideas to the Discussion.

3) Limiting the claims about changes and the lack of changes in the mutant, perhaps by focusing on the idea that one kinematic measure was preserved while others (interlimb and intralimb) were not.

4) Providing a better description of the construction of the passive model, and (if feasible) providing a physical model (or explaining why this was not done).

5) Addressing the point either experimentally or with clarification of the (apparently) very low N (=3) for the pcd mice.

6) Improving presentation of the results/figures/sequence of calling figures, as indicated in the reviews.

Reviewer #1:

1) The authors emphasize in several places that 'traditional' measures of kinematics are unimpaired in mutants. I found this to be overly-simplistic, at least based on the results presented here. As I understand it, the main consistency is in the x-axis forward paw motion, while there are changes in vertical and mediolateral paw motion and in joint angles. Changes in vertical paw trajectory and joint angles are hardly 'non-traditional', 'complex', or even '3D' and all measures are definitely 'individual-limb'. This point is made several times in the text (see points below) and seems unwarranted. I'm not saying the results aren't interesting, nor do I think that these conclusions are necessary for the impact of the paper – I just don't think that this conclusion as stated is supported.

2) On a similar point, it's not clear to me that any of their measures are really looking at within-limb coordination, at least as this is usually considered. Most of the measures relate to paw movement, whereas traditionally issues of coordination (e.g. in studies examining the role of the cerebellum, as cited in the paper) consider interactions between joints. Yet these analyses really aren't done here. They show that joint angles are apparently different in the animals, but these are for single joints as opposed to joint angle relationships (and what those angles are is unclear, see below). I don't think that the results shown here rule out a possible deficit in traditional, within-limb coordination. I think this is mainly an issue of presentation, however, rather than one of substance. As stated above, I don't think the impact of the paper relies on this conclusion and it could be made more precise without loss of significance.

3) I potentially like the analysis of nose and tail passive movements very much, but I did have a few issues with it. First, although the results are consistent with a role of the cerebellum in predictive control based on forward models, they're not really a direct demonstration thereof. A more direct demonstration might involve examining adaptations to perturbations, e.g. adding a weight to the tail and seeing that initially control animals look like mutants but then learn to predict and compensate for this, whereas mutants never do so. Also, could the results simply be interpreted as one of a limited capacity for motor control? e.g. mutants have limited capacity for producing locomotion and expend most of it on x-axis movement of the paw since it's critical for task performance, whereas other aspects of behavior are allowed to vary? I appreciate the authors are careful on this point to say that the results are 'consistent' with this idea, but alternative explanations might be considered more directly.

4) For the nose/tail passive analysis, I originally thought that this was an actual physical model, rather than the geometric model used here. It seems clear that a physical model is the better way to do this. Why wasn't it done? The geometric model, with its assumptions of lags taken from data which is actually observed, seems more indirect and therefore less compelling. Finally, as I understand it (and I might have missed it), this analysis was only done for the mutants. It would be very good to have done the same analysis for the control animals and show that the tail/nose movements are inconsistent with passive movement, e.g. it could have been that the movement of the pelvic girdle was different in controls, leading to less tail movement (even though the hindlimbs are in alternation for both controls and mutants).

Reviewer #2:

The paper by Machado et al. examines gait patterns in wildtype and Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mice using a novel system for tracking locomotor kinematics in freely walking mice. The authors conclude that the individual limb kinematics of pcd mice are normal when the weight and the walking speed of the mice are taken into account. In contrast, pcd mice have impaired coordination of movements across joints, limbs and body. These results are interpreted as evidence that the cerebellum provides a forward model. This is a strong paper. I commend the authors for wrestling with a complex dataset and extracting from it a number of thought-provoking findings. I personally found many of the results exciting, but I must admit that I'm not an expert in the field of locomotion or ataxia. It was not always clear if a particular result in the paper was a major advance or just confirmation of something we already knew. For this reason, I think that it's important for the authors to clarify and emphasize the significance of their results throughout the text. I've given two examples below:

1) It is remarkable that in wildtype mice, one can account for upwards of 80% of the variance in kinematic parameters like stride length, swing velocity and cadence, simply by taking into account the walking speed and the weight of the mouse. Is this a new approach? In their rebuttal, the authors mention that the Cendelin et al. (2010) paper found that all the gait differences between lurcher and control mice disappeared when they corrected for walking speed. Did Cendelin et al. make the correction using a similar modeling approach?

2) One of the main findings is that individual limb movements of pcd mice are relatively spared (when weight and walking speed are taken into account), whereas interlimb coordination is impaired. It is not clear how much of this we already knew. For example, in the subsection “Front-hind Interlimb coordination is specifically impaired in pcd”, the authors mention that previous studies in ataxic mice have failed to detect any impairments in the kinematic parameters of individual limbs. Did those studies not examine interlimb coordination as well? If the authors are the first to show that mice with cerebellar deficits have a specific impairment in locomotor coordination but not in movement of individual limbs, this is a big deal.

Additional recommendations to help make an already strong paper even stronger:

3) Drop the emphasis on forward models. The authors argue that the deficits they've uncovered point to a lack of a forward model in pcd mice. Although I found some of the evidence presented intriguing (for example the analysis of tail movements), it is far from conclusive. Furthermore, it is difficult to reconcile the normal individual limb kinematics with a faulty forward model – individual limbs are controlled by multiple agonist/antagonist muscles whose coordination requires well-calibrated forward models. I think the authors can still interpret their results in the context of forward/inverse models, but I strongly recommend that they save this interpretation for the Discussion, tone it down a bit and address the limitations. The paper would be stronger if the second paragraph of the Introduction is rewritten to highlight the main questions to be addressed in the paper, instead of offering to resolve controversies about forward vs inverse cerebellar models.

4) Analysis of variability: All the analyses are based on average data. For example, Figure 3B-E shows that there is no difference in the individual limb kinematics of pcd mice and sized-matched controls. But this is done only for the average kinematic values. Is it not possible that pcd mice might show increased trial-to-trial variability in their movements relative to sized-matched controls? How would such a finding change the authors' conclusions?

Reviewer #3:

The authors developed a machine learning algorithm to track the individual limbs as well as the nose and tail of mice in 3D during natural, voluntary locomotion. They provide a very detailed analysis of locomotion parameters in control and ataxic Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mice, revealing that individual limb kinematics in pcd mice are not different from control mice when accounting for the mouse's weight and speed, but that pcd mice present multi-joint and inter-limb-coordination deficits. The study has been carefully conducted and provides new and useful tools for measuring and analyzing specific features of locomotion and ataxia with unprecedented accuracy.

1) The construction of the "passive model" (Figure 5) is unclear. For example, does this model take into account the mass of the tail? Please describe in more detail how the passive prediction is calculated.

2) The authors contrast the forward model with an inverse kinematic model in the Introduction. What do they think the inverse kinematic model would predict and how does this contrast with their findings?

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "A quantitative framework for whole-body coordination reveals specific deficits in freely walking ataxic mice" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers. The manuscript has been greatly improved and the revision was met with enthusiasm. There are only a few remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

In particular, the manual joint-angle analysis shown in Figure 3H seems limited by the single animal in each condition, and discussion among reviewers and editors led to the consensus that it could simply be dropped without major impact on the manuscript. We therefore recommend cutting this one measurement and illustration. Alternatively, if there is some reason why a single animal in each category is of value, please justify the experiment clearly. This point is explained further below.

In the subsection “Individual limb parameters”, the description makes it seem like one pcd animal and one control were used for this analysis. If so, this seems very questionable and underpowered. I'd be willing to bet that, with enough n, it would be possible to find a significant difference between two different weight matched controls. I'm not sure how the stats behave in this situation, but it's not clear to me how mixed models would be able to partition variance due to random effects (individual subjects) from the fixed effects (mutation) if there were only one animal in each group. It seems that for other comparisons with weight matched controls much larger N's are used, whereas this analysis is limited because of the need to hand mark frames. It might be easiest to simply drop this joint angle analysis – I don't think its omission would change the impact of the paper. Also, shouldn't it be ‘knee, heel, toe’? And here it's stated that the angle of the foot and arm relative to the ground are quantified – I might have missed it, but I wasn't sure where that was reported in the Results.

claims.source: Each parameter measured, including stride length, cadence, swing velocity, and stance duration (Figure 2C–F), varied consistently with the walking speed of the mouse.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2 showing systematic relationships between these parameters and speed.

claims.claim: Basic stride parameters in mice can be predicted based solely on walking speed and body weight.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that the value of each stride parameter was readily predicted based solely on walking speed and body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the linear mixed-effects models presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pcd mice are smaller than control mice.
claims.source: Since pcd mice, like many ataxic animals, are smaller than controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: This is shown in the data comparing body weights between pcd and control mice.

claims.claim: Pcd mice walk more slowly than control mice.
claims.source: and given that they walk more slowly (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the histogram of walking speeds in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The instantaneous forward paw velocity profiles of pcd mice are not distinguishable from those of size-matched controls across speeds.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the instantaneous forward paw velocity profiles of pcd mice were not distinguishable from those of size-matched controls, across speeds (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E comparing velocity profiles between pcd and size-matched controls.

claims.claim: Pcd mice exhibit a wider base of support than size-matched control mice.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings of ataxic mice and humans, pcd mice exhibited a wider base of support than size-matched control mice (Figure 3F) (F(15.51,1)=42.87, p <0 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3F and supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Pcd mice show significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws across speeds.
claims.source: Further, analysis of the vertical (z) trajectories revealed significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws of pcd mice, across speeds (F(66.84,1)=17.16, p <0 0.001) (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H with statistical support.

claims.claim: Wildtype mice walk in a symmetrical trot pattern across speeds.
claims.source: In our experiments, wildtype mice walked in a symmetrical trot pattern across speeds—each diagonal pair of limbs moved together and alternated with the other pair (Figure 4A, left).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the polar plots and support patterns in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination is markedly disrupted in pcd due to specific changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs.
claims.source: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination was markedly disrupted in pcd, due to specific and consistent changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs (F(77.07,1) = 4.11, p <0 0.05; Figure 4A, right; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and 4B with statistical support.

claims.claim: Left-right alternation is maintained in pcd mice.
claims.source: Importantly, in marked contrast to the front-hind limb coupling, left-right alternation was maintained in pcd (F(159,1) = 0.018, p=0.89; Figure 4A, right: red vs blue and cyan vs magenta; Figure 4B, left).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis in Figure 4 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Pcd mice spend more time with more paws on the ground.
claims.source: Pcd mice spent more time with more paws on the ground (Figure 4D, right; Figure 4E, left) (3-paw support F(82,1) = 83.57, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the support pattern analysis in Figure 4D and 4E with statistical support.

claims.claim: The walking speed of pcd mice is limited by the need to have at least one hind paw on the ground for postural stability.
claims.source: In other words, it appears that the walking speed of pcd mice is limited by the need to have at least one hind paw on the ground, for postural stability (Stolze et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the observation that pcd walking speeds coincide with the transition from positive to negative % double hind limb supports, as shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Pcd mice show an increase in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support.
claims.source: Despite their slower walking speeds and increased percent of time spent with more paws on the ground, pcd mice also showed an increase in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support (Figure 4E, right; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (F(46.78,1) = 7.76, p = 0.01)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4E with statistical support.

claims.claim: The distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position is more variable in pcd mice.
claims.source: While the average distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position was the same in pcd and controls (F(14,1) = 0.44, p = 0.52), it was more variable in pcd (F(168,1) = 75.30, p < 0.001; Figure 4G), across speeds.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G with statistical support.

claims.claim: Both the nose and tail of pcd mice exhibit large side-to-side oscillations during the locomotor cycle.
claims.source: In control mice, lateral movements of the nose and tail were small (Figure 5A,B, black). In striking contrast, however, both the nose and the tail of pcd mice exhibited large side-to-side oscillations during the locomotor cycle (Figure 5A,B, purple; Video 2) (compared to size-matched controls: nose F(13.48,1) = 5.49, p < 0.05, tail F(415,1) = 91.01, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and 5B with statistical support.

claims.claim: In pcd mice, both nose and tail become increasingly phase-lagged at faster speeds.
claims.source: However, in pcd both nose and tail (Figure 5E) became increasingly phase-lagged at faster speeds (tail: F(401.02,1) = 5.55,p <0 0.05; nose: F(53.61,1) = 4.89,p <0 0.05 for speeds above 0.1 m/s).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with statistical support.

claims.claim: Tail movements in pcd can be modeled as passive consequences of the forward movement of the hind limbs.
claims.source: The large, sinusoidal amplitude of the tail oscillations and their time-delayed relationship to hind paw movement suggested to us that tail movements in pcd could reflect passive consequences of the forward movement of the hind limbs.
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is tested with a geometric model presented in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claims.claim: The side-to-side tail movements predicted by the passive model are strikingly similar to the tail oscillations of pcd mice.
claims.source: The side-to-side tail movements predicted by the passive model were strikingly similar to the tail oscillations of pcd mice (compare grey dashed lines with purple traces in Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison between model predictions and actual data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The tail oscillations of pcd mice are fit very well with a passive model that incorporates a 31 ms time delay for the base of the tail plus a fixed delay per additional tail segment.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5F, the tail oscillations of pcd mice were fit very well, across walking speeds and tail segments, with a passive model that incorporated a 31 ms time delay for the base of the tail (reflecting the initial inertia of the mouse's rear) plus a fixed delay per additional tail segment (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5F showing the model fit to the data.

claims.claim: Nose movements in pcd are consistent with a time-delayed (96 ms) side-to-side movement.
claims.source: A similar model for the nose (Figure 5) was also consistent with a time-delayed (96 ms) side-to-side nose movement in pcd.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the model presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
claims.source: Thus, in pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the successful modeling of nose and tail movements as passive consequences of hindlimb motion.

claims.claim: Tail and nose movements must be actively canceled in wildtype mice to keep the body axis aligned for forward movement.
claims.source: Further, our results suggest that this movement must be actively canceled in wildtype mice to keep the body axis aligned for forward movement.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wildtype mice do not show the oscillations predicted by the passive model, while pcd mice do.

claims.claim: In control mice, the movement of different parts of the body is synchronized.
claims.source: During locomotion in control mice, the movement of different parts of the body is synchronized, and vertical nose and tail movements are relatively small (Figure 6A, left).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the ribbon plots in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In pcd, spatial and temporal coordination across the body is dramatically impaired.
claims.source: In pcd, however, spatial and temporal coordination across the body is dramatically impaired (Figure 6A, right).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A showing desynchronized movements across body parts.

claims.claim: In control mice, the movement of most body parts is either strongly correlated or anti-correlated.
claims.source: Finally, a correlation analysis reveals that in control mice, the movement of most body parts is either strongly correlated or anti-correlated (i.e. they move either in–or out-of phase with each other; Figure 6B, left, red and blue).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the correlation matrix in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In pcd mice, the correlations between body part movements are weaker and more variable.
claims.source: In pcd mice, however, the correlations are weaker and more variable (Figure 6B, right).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the correlation matrix in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The lack of correlational structure in pcd reflects the failure to synchronize the movements of different parts of the body.
claims.source: This lack of correlational structure reflects the failure of pcd mice to synchronize the movements of different parts of the body.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the correlation analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Ataxic pcd mice have specific deficits in coordinating movement in three dimensions across joints, limbs, and body.
claims.source: Taken together, the results of Figures 3–6 suggest that while the forward motion of individual paws is largely spared, ataxic pcd mice have specific deficits in coordinating movement in three dimensions across joints, limbs, and body.
claims.evidence: This conclusion synthesizes the findings from Figures 3-6.

claims.claim: Many existing analyses of mouse locomotion fail to capture the essence of the coordination deficits of ataxic mice.
claims.source: Therefore it has not been clear to what extent exisiting analyses of mouse locomotion capture the essence of the coordination deficits of ataxic mice that are so visible to the human eye (Cendelin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the current study and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Failure to account for differences in walking speed and body size when comparing data across mice can lead to nonspecific effects being misinterpreted as symptoms of ataxia.
claims.source: This important result highlights that failure to account for differences in walking speed and body size when comparing data across mice and strides can lead to nonspecific effects being misinterpreted as symptoms of ataxia (Koopmans et al., 2007; Cendelin et al., 2010; Wuehr et al., 2012; Batka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that stride parameters in pcd are normal when accounting for speed and body size, and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Left-right alternation during locomotion is generated within the spinal cord itself.
claims.source: Interestingly, while front-hind paw coupling was dramatically altered in pcd, left-right alternation was preserved entirely, consistent with the idea that such alternation is generated within the spinal cord itself (Crone et al., 2009; Kiehn, 2011; Dougherty et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the preservation of left-right alternation in pcd and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The major neuroanatomical finding in pcd is the complete postnatal degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and subsequent loss of granule cells and related structures.
claims.source: The major neuroanatomical finding in pcd is the complete postnatal degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and subsequent loss of granule cells and related structures (Mullen et al., 1976; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Morton and Bastian, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The preservation of forward paw motion in pcd likely reflects the presence of compensatory mechanisms resulting from the chronic loss of Purkinje cells.
claims.source: The most likely interpretation of the surprisingly intact forward paw motion in pcd is that it reflects the presence of inevitable compensatory mechanisms resulting from the chronic loss of Purkinje cells.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The cerebellum provides internal models for motor control.
claims.source: While many lines of evidence suggest that the cerebellum provides internal models for motor control (Wolpert et al., 1998; Ito, 2008), there has been disagreement about the nature of these models (Ebner and Pasalar, 2008; Medina, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claims.claim: The cerebellum may act as an inverse model that computes a command to achieve desired movement.
claims.source: Studies from some systems, including eye movements, have suggested that the cerebellum acts as an inverse model that computes a command to achieve desired movement (Shidara et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The cerebellum may provide a forward model that predicts the consequences of movements.
claims.source: Other work, particularly on reaching movements, the cerebellar-like nuclei of electric fish, and locomotor adaptation, has suggested that the cerebellum provides a forward model that predicts the consequences of movements (Bastian et al., 1996; Kennedy et al., 2014) (Pasalar et al., 2006) (Morton and Bastian, 2006).
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is cited from previous literature.

claims.claim: The absence of forward models could form the basis for impaired coordination associated with gait ataxia in mice.
claims.source: Therefore our results raise the intriguing possibility that the absence of forward models, rather than a failure to execute appropriate movement kinematics per se, could form the basis for impaired coordination associated with gait ataxia in mice.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The specific features of gait ataxia vary across mouse models.
claims.source: Although cerebellar involvement is a shared feature across ataxic mouse mutants, the details of the motor phenotypes are different for different mutations (Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Patients with cerebellar damage exhibit varying degrees and features of ataxia.
claims.source: Similarly, patients with cerebellar damage exhibit varying degrees and features of ataxia (Morton and Bastian, 2003, 2007; Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Cadence and stride length increase with walking speed in mice.
claims.source: Cadence and stride length increased with walking speed, indicating that faster walking in mice is associated with longer, more frequent strides (Clarke and Still, 1999; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Batka et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Swing velocity increases linearly with walking speed.

claims.claim: Stance duration decreases steeply with increasing walking speed.

claims.claim: Adding age or gender did not improve predictions of stride parameters once body size was taken into account.
claims.source: While basic stride parameters also varied with gender and age, these effects were related to differences in body size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); adding neither age nor gender improved the predictions once body size was taken into account.

claims.claim: Pcd mice can be easily identified by eye based on their ataxic, uncoordinated movements.
claims.source: Pcd mice can be easily identified by eye based on their ataxic, uncoordinated movements (Mullen et al., 1976; Le Marec and Lalonde, 1997).

claims.claim: Pcd mice exhibit impaired rotarod performance.

claims.claim: The motor deficits of pcd mice are relatively mild compared to other spontaneous ataxic mutants.

claims.claim: Peak swing velocities increased with faster walking speeds but did not vary by genotype.

claims.source: Further, analysis of the vertical (z) trajectories revealed significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws of pcd mice, across speeds (F(66.84,1)=17.16, p <0 0.001) (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: The variability of vertical displacement was not different in pcd.

claims.claim: At slower speeds wildtype mice showed a tendency toward a 'walking trot'.

claims.claim: There was no abrupt shift between gait patterns—stance phases varied smoothly with walking speed and duty cycle.

claims.claim: In control mice, both the tail and nose were phase-locked to the stride cycle across walking speeds.

claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

results.result: The authors developed LocoMouse, a novel automated system for analyzing 3D locomotor kinematics in freely walking mice. The system uses high-speed cameras (400 fps), a mirror setup, machine learning algorithms (SVM classifiers), and automated tracking to capture paw, nose, and tail movements with 2.5 ms temporal resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C48-C53, and C84-C88 collectively describe the LocoMouse system's technical specifications, capabilities, and validation. The system is well-documented with detailed methods (C99-C102), visual evidence (Figure 1), and validation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing high correlation between automated and manual tracking (r=0.982-1.0 for x,y,z coordinates). The tracking failure rate was <10% (C101), and the system successfully tracked multiple body parts in 3D.

results.result: Basic stride parameters (stride length, cadence, swing velocity, stance duration) in wildtype mice can be accurately predicted based solely on walking speed and body weight, with no additional predictive value from age or gender once body size is accounted for.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C54-C59 are strongly supported by comprehensive data from 34 wildtype mice with diverse ages (30-114 days) and weights (7-33g), totaling 9,602 strides. Linear mixed-effects models show high R² values (0.83-0.95) for predictions based on speed and weight (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The statistical approach is rigorous, using likelihood ratio tests to compare models and demonstrating that adding age or gender does not improve predictions (C59).

results.result: Despite being visibly ataxic, pcd mice show normal forward paw motion when accounting for their smaller body size and slower walking speed. Stride parameters and forward velocity profiles are indistinguishable from size-matched controls, and variability in some parameters (cadence, stance duration) is actually reduced in pcd.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C11-C13 are well-supported by data comparing pcd mice (N=3, n=3,052 strides) to size-matched controls (N=11, n=3,400 strides). The linear mixed-effects models accurately predict pcd stride parameters based on speed and body size (Figure 3B-D). Statistical tests confirm no differences in forward velocity profiles (F(10.97,1)=0.092, p=0.77, C66) and stride length (F(14,1)=0.70, p=0.42). The finding that cadence and stance duration are less variable in pcd (C65) is statistically significant (p<0.05) and surprising, strengthening the conclusion that forward motion is preserved.

results.result: Pcd mice show specific impairments in off-axis (3D) paw movements, including a wider base of support and significantly larger vertical displacement of paws during swing, though the variability of vertical displacement is unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C14-C15, and C68-C69 are supported by statistical analyses showing significant differences in base of support (F(15.51,1)=42.87, p<0.001, C14) and vertical displacement (F(66.84,1)=17.16, p<0.001, C15/C68) between pcd and size-matched controls. The data are visualized in Figure 3F-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The finding that variability is unchanged (C69) is also statistically supported (F(81,1)=2.47, p=0.12), indicating consistent but altered 3D trajectories.

results.result: Interlimb coordination is specifically disrupted in pcd mice, with altered front-hind phasing but preserved left-right alternation. Pcd mice spend more time with more paws on the ground, show increased unstable support configurations, and exhibit more variable paw placement, though the changes in phasing are consistent rather than more variable.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 and C70-C76 are comprehensively supported by detailed analyses of interlimb coordination (Figure 4). Statistical tests confirm altered front-hind phasing (F(77.07,1)=4.11, p<0.05, C17) while left-right alternation is preserved (F(159,1)=0.018, p=0.89, C18). The increased 3-paw support (F(82,1)=83.57, p<0.001, C19) and unstable 2-paw configurations (F(46.78,1)=7.76, p=0.01, C21) are statistically significant. The finding that phasing is less variable in pcd (C74-C75) strengthens the interpretation that deficits are specific and consistent rather than random.

results.result: Nose and tail movements in pcd mice exhibit large side-to-side oscillations that can be accurately modeled as passive consequences of forward hindlimb motion with fixed time delays (31 ms for tail base, 96 ms for nose). This suggests that wildtype mice actively cancel these passive movements to maintain body alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C30 and C77-C83 are strongly supported by both empirical data and geometric modeling. Statistical tests confirm significantly larger oscillations in pcd (tail: F(415,1)=91.01, p<0.001; nose: F(13.48,1)=5.49, p<0.05, C23) and speed-dependent phase lags (C24). The passive geometric model (C25-C28, C79-C80) accurately predicts the observed oscillations (Figure 5, Video 3). The argument that hindlimb differences cannot explain the oscillations is supported by data showing preserved hindpaw alternation (C81) and double support (C82), and model predictions about base of support effects (C83). The inference that wildtype mice actively cancel these movements (C30) is logical but remains speculative.

results.result: Whole-body coordination is dramatically impaired in pcd mice, with desynchronized movements across body parts and weaker, more variable correlations between body part movements compared to the strong correlations or anti-correlations observed in control mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are supported by visualization and correlation analyses of vertical trajectories across body parts (Figure 6). The ribbon plots (Figure 6A) clearly show synchronized movements in controls versus desynchronized movements in pcd. The correlation matrices (Figure 6B) quantitatively demonstrate the loss of correlational structure in pcd. This result synthesizes findings from Figures 3-6 and provides a comprehensive view of coordination deficits across joints, limbs, and body.

results.result: The coordination deficits in pcd are consistent with a failure to predict and compensate for the consequences of movement across the body, suggesting that the cerebellum provides forward models for motor control rather than simply executing movement kinematics.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C38-C39, C41, and C45 represent interpretations and hypotheses based on the data. While the passive model of tail/nose movements (C6) is well-supported, the broader interpretation about forward models (C45) is speculative. The preservation of left-right alternation (C39) and forward paw motion (C41) are cited as evidence for spinal and compensatory mechanisms, but these interpretations, while plausible, go beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The hypothesis about forward models is interesting and consistent with the data, but would require additional experiments to confirm.

results.result: Many existing analyses of mouse locomotion rely on indirect measures that lack specificity and fail to capture the essence of coordination deficits visible in ataxic mice during overground locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C89-C91 are supported by extensive citations to previous literature and are consistent with the motivation for developing LocoMouse. The authors demonstrate through their own data that basic stride parameters (which are commonly measured) fail to capture ataxia when speed and body size are not accounted for (C38), supporting the claim that existing approaches are insufficient. However, this is primarily a literature-based claim rather than a direct experimental finding of the current study.

results.result: Background knowledge about cerebellar function, pcd mouse anatomy, and theories of cerebellar motor control (inverse vs. forward models) is accurately cited from the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C40, C42-C44, C46-C47, and C92 are all cited from previous literature and represent established knowledge or existing hypotheses. These claims provide context for the current study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: The experimental design included appropriate animal subjects (wildtype C57BL/6 mice, pcd mice, and littermate controls), adequate sample sizes, and proper ethical approvals.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 and C103 describe the experimental subjects and procedures. Sample sizes are adequate for the wildtype group (N=34 mice, n=9,602 strides) but relatively small for pcd mice (N=3 mice, n=3,052 strides). However, the use of size-matched controls (N=11, n=3,400 strides) from the larger wildtype dataset is appropriate. The consideration of extra-cerebellar degeneration after P50 (C98) and separate analysis of young pcd mice shows methodological rigor. Ethical approvals are documented (C103).
